# Explainer: Is reformism still relevant in Iran?

All from Iran All International 25 February 2026 12:55 GMT Copy URL to clipboard Bookmark Article

## Overview

Reformism in Iran – the belief that meaningful democratic change can be achieved through the Islamic Republic's own institutions - is facing its gravest crisis since it first attracted voters in 1997.

The bloody unrest that peaked in early January has not only shaken the political establishment, but has fractured the reformist camp itself. Some reformist figures condemned the crackdown and even questioned the foundations of the system. Others highlighted "external conspiracies" while expressing sorrow over the violence. Several others have been temporarily detained.

As Iran becomes more polarised, many are asking whether reformism still has relevance - or whether it has reached the end of its political road.

## The birth of a movement

The reform movement first came to prominence with the surprise election of the cleric and former culture minister Mohammad Khatami in 1997.

Running on promises of political liberalisation, rule of law and engagement with the West, Khatami won nearly 70% of the vote on a record turnout. His victory was widely described as the start of a " Tehran Spring".

Newspapers flourished, civil society organisations expanded, and women and young voters felt newly empowered. Internationally, Khatami promoted his idea of a " Dialogue Among Civilisations".

But the optimism soon collided with the reality of Iran's system of "dual power". While presidents and parliament are elected, key elements of authority remain vested in unelected institutions run by Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei - the judiciary, the state broadcaster, the security services and the Guardian Council, which vets candidates and can block legislation.

A hostile establishment meant reformist bills were rejected, newspapers shut down and allies of Khatami prosecuted. A shadowy series of killings targeting dissident intellectuals – known as the " chain murders" – showed the hard limits of tolerance.

Although Khatami won a second term, many of his promises remained unfulfilled by the time he left office in 2005. Critics within his own camp argued that his instinct for compromise and reluctance to mobilise his popular base had allowed hardliners to outmanoeuvre him.

The reformists had boosted the Islamic Republic's popular legitimacy. But their inability to shift the balance of power left many supporters disillusioned.

## Hardline return and the Green rupture

In 2005, turnout dropped sharply, with no reformist candidate reaching the run-off. The eventual winner, Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, presented himself as a populist outsider and ushered in a more confrontational era.

Reformists were marginalised in parliament and government, while tensions with the West escalated over Iran's nuclear programme. 

The movement found new energy in 2009 behind former prime minister Mir Hossein Mousavi. His campaign revived the spirit of 1997, drawing massive rallies and a record turnout.

When Ahmadinejad was declared the winner in a landslide, allegations of vote manipulation spread rapidly. Hundreds of thousands took to the streets in what became known as the Iranian Green Movement – the largest protests since 1979.

The demonstrations were crushed. Mousavi, his wife Zahra Rahnavard and fellow opposition leader Mehdi Karroubi were placed under house arrest.

The crackdown marked a turning point. Reformism had mobilised millions, but it could not translate its popularity into power.

## Years in the wilderness

In the aftermath of 2009, the movement fragmented. Some reformists boycotted the 2012 parliamentary elections, which they saw as engineered, while others argued that participation was the only way to preserve influence.

They regrouped behind the pragmatic cleric Hassan Rouhani in 2013. Although not formally a reformist, he campaigned on moderation and international engagement.

His landmark achievement was the 2015 nuclear agreement, the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), which eased sanctions in exchange for limits on Iran's nuclear activities.

Reformists also regained further confidence after many of their candidates won seats in both the parliamentary and Assembly of Experts elections in 2016, following Khatami's callout to voters.

But domestic reform remained limited. The December 2017–January 2018 unrest exposed public frustration with both conservative and reformist camps

When the US withdrew from the nuclear deal in 2018, Iran's economy deteriorated sharply. 

In November 2019, protests over fuel prices were met with a violent crackdown. Hundreds were killed, according to human rights groups. Reformists allied to the government appeared powerless to prevent the bloodshed or distance themselves from it, further eroding public trust.

## From hardline consolidation to snap elections

By 2021, the Guardian Council had disqualified most prominent reformist candidates. The hardline cleric Ebrahim Raisi won the presidency on a record low turnout.

Reformist influence shrank sharply. Key figures boycotted the March 2024 parliamentary elections, and even Khatami joined them, describing his decision not to vote as a protest and a show of solidarity with other reformists.

After Raisi's sudden death in 2024, the authorities allowed the reformist-aligned politician Massoud Pezeshkian to run in the snap election – a move widely interpreted as an attempt to raise participation.

Backed by the Reform Front umbrella group and Khatami, Pezeshkian won. But turnout was historically low, underlining deep public disengagement. Pezeshkian positioned himself as being loyal to the supreme leader, and not a challenger of the system's fundamentals.

## From Mahsa protests to January unrest

The 2022 protests triggered by the death in custody of Mahsa Amini had already exposed a generational shift. Many young protesters rejected both conservatives and reformists, calling for sweeping structural change.

By late 2025, economic hardship and currency devaluation ignited another wave of unrest. Demonstrations that began over living conditions escalated into broader anti-establishment protests.

They peaked on 8-9 January 2026, after calls for mobilisation by the exiled former crown prince Reza Pahlavi. What followed was described by rights groups as the deadliest crackdown in the Islamic Republic's history.

Reformist reactions were divided. Mousavi, distanced from the ruling establishment, called for a constitutional referendum and a peaceful transfer of power. Other prominent figures, including Mostafa Tajzadeh, echoed calls for fundamental change.

Azar Mansouri, head of the Reform Front, expressed " disgust and rage" over the violence. Many dissident voices, including former reformists, backed Mousavi's proposal for a broad-based " salvation front" against "despotism and foreign war".

Others were more cautious. While expressing sorrow over the violence and renewing his calls for reform, Khatami also accused Israel and the US of pursuing "external conspiracies" intended to undermine Iranian unity

President Pezeshkian expressed sympathy with protesters but later echoed official language about "riots" and foreign interference while calling for investigations.

 He criticised a prominent reformist figure who had accused security forces of engineering violence during the unrest to justify the ensuing crackdown.

The authorities also widened their crackdown to include reformist critics, detaining several of them temporarily for "propaganda against the system".

## An existential dilemma

Reformism is facing an existential crisis after the January unrest exposed its core dilemma. The movement had long argued that gradual, insider change could safeguard stability while expanding freedoms, but years of crackdowns and mismanagement under different governments have led many Iranians to conclude that elected officials hold little real power.

Through supressing dissent and curbing the scope for meaningful change, the establishment has degraded the mechanism that once channelled public frustration into participation. And now even more radical reformists find themselves overtaken by a protest movement that increasingly challenges the Islamic Republic itself. 

Reformists now face stark options: continue to pursue limited gains within the system, attempt to redefine the movement for a new generation, or risk further splintering as anti‑establishment currents grow stronger. Nearly three decades after its rise, reformism stands at a crossroads, unsure whether it can reinvent itself or whether the country has simply moved on from the idea of gradual reform.
